Before Day 1 3 min

How 20 minutes beats an hour

Each day you watch one Crash Course episode, about 10 minutes, and spend the other 10 doing the things that make it stick. Rereading and highlighting feel productive but barely help. Testing yourself and coming back later help most.

Retrieval practice strong evidence

Pulling an answer out of memory beats reading it again. That's why every answer here is hidden until you've tried.

Spacing strong

Reviewing after a little forgetting builds durable memory. The warm-up review does this for you automatically.

Guess first moderate

A wrong prediction before the video primes your attention. Wrong guesses are useful data, not failures.

Interleaving moderate

Psychology and philosophy alternate, so you keep comparing two ways of attacking the same question.

Your cue: pick one fixed moment, like "after morning chai, before Instagram", and do Step 1 there. On bad days, run rescue mode: the review plus the video, 12 minutes. Missing a day doesn't break anything. Just pick up the next one.

Learn one field, or both

Both fields alternate by default. Want to go deep on one first? Pick it here or on the side tabs. The other field's days hide, and your warm-up reviews switch to that field only. The plan has 12 psychology days and 16 philosophy days, so a single field is a shorter, sharper track.

The map · read once, come back often

Two fields, one mind

Philosophy asks the questions. Psychology tests the ones it can. Here's the territory, the timeline and what professionals actually believe.

Map 1

Psychology's family tree

Five core branches, three applied ones and two lenses that cut across all of them. Every Crash Course episode sits on one of these branches.

Map 2

Philosophy's family tree

Two halves (how things are, what matters), one shared toolkit (logic) and three great traditions. Crash Course covers the Western one. You'll get the other two as insider notes.

Indian philosophy in one minute

Nyaya

Logic and epistemology. Four sources of knowledge: perception, inference, comparison, testimony.

Samkhya + Yoga

Dualism of consciousness (purusha) and matter (prakriti). Yoga adds the practice.

Vedanta

Readings of the Upanishads and the Gita. Advaita (Shankara) is non-dual. Not simply "everything is illusion".

Buddhism

No permanent self (anatta). Nagarjuna: things lack intrinsic essence, which is not the same as nothing existing.

Jainism

Anekantavada: reality is many-sided, so any single view is partial. An ancient cure for confirmation bias.

Charvaka

Materialists: only perception counts, no karma, no rebirth. India's original sceptics.

"Astika and nastika means accepting Vedic authority or not, not theist versus atheist. Samkhya can be non-theistic and still astika."

Map 3

2,800 years in three lanes

Philosophy ran in parallel in Greece, India and China. Psychology broke away in the 1800s when someone started measuring.

Map 4

Where the two fields meet

The same five questions run through the whole course. Philosophy sharpens each one, psychology brings data.

    Day 1 · Philosophy Philosophy track · 1 of 16 about 20 min

    What is philosophy?

    Philosophy is what you do with a question you can't settle by looking it up or running an experiment yet. Physics, psychology and economics all started here and moved out once they found a method. What's left is the hard stuff: what's real, what counts as knowing, and what's worth doing.

    BaselineOn a scale of 1 to 5, how well could you explain to a CEO what psychology and philosophy each study, and how they differ? Write the number down. You'll rate yourself again at the end of Week 1.

    2 · Predict first · 2 min

    What makes a question philosophical, and why should a founder care?

    Guess firstTrue or false: philosophy is mostly personal opinions about the meaning of life.

    Show answer
    False. Philosophy is about arguments: claims backed by reasons anyone can inspect and attack. Opinions are where it starts, not where it ends.

    Guess firstDid physics and psychology start inside philosophy?

    Show answer
    Both did. Newton's great book was called Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy (1687). Psychology left when Wundt opened his lab in 1879.

    Five words to know before you press play:

    Metaphysicswhat is real: mind, self, time, free will, God
    Epistemologyhow we know anything, and when belief is justified
    Value theoryethics, politics, aesthetics: what matters
    Logicthe rules for which reasons actually support a conclusion
    Socratic methodquestioning someone until their hidden assumptions show

    What is Philosophy?

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Crash Course starts in Athens. Insiders don't. Systematic philosophy appeared in India (the Upanishads, the Buddha, Nyaya logic) and China (Confucius, Laozi) in the same centuries as Greece. Indian philosophy in particular is obsessed with epistemology: how many reliable sources of knowledge (pramanas) are there?
    • Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we know comes second-hand from Plato, Xenophon and the comic playwright Aristophanes. When someone quotes Socrates, they're usually quoting Plato's character.
    • Philosophers disagree, on the record. The 2020 PhilPapers Survey asked 1,785 philosophers 100 questions. Example: 59% lean compatibilist on free will and 67% lean atheist, yet 62% are moral realists. The field is a map of the best arguments, not a consensus.
    • Analytic vs continental is a style split, not two teams. Analytic work prizes tight arguments and distinctions. Continental work (phenomenology, existentialism, critical theory) puts lived experience, history and power centre stage. Insiders ask "what problem, what method?" instead of "which camp?"
    Socratesc. 470-399 BCE. Turned questioning into a method, and was executed for it.
    Nagarjunac. 150-250 CE. Indian Buddhist philosopher whose logic of "emptiness" still has analytic philosophers arguing.

    "Before we argue the answer: is this a question about facts, about definitions, or about values?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words, explain to a smart 15-year-old what philosophy is and how it differs from science.

    Compare with a model answer
    Philosophy works on questions we can't yet settle by measuring: what's real, what counts as knowing, what we ought to do. It answers with arguments that anyone can check and attack. Science grew out of it. Once a question gets a reliable method of measurement, it usually leaves philosophy and becomes its own field.

    Name philosophy's three big areas and the toolkit underneath.

    Show answer
    Metaphysics (what's real), epistemology (how we know), value theory (ethics, politics, aesthetics), with logic as the shared toolkit.

    Why do we only know Socrates second-hand?

    Show answer
    He wrote nothing. We know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, mostly Plato.

    What separates a philosophical position from an opinion?

    Show answer
    A position comes with an argument that can be stated, tested and objected to. An opinion doesn't have to.

    A cofounder says: "AI will replace all agencies within five years." Before you argue, what kind of question is it?

    Show a model answer
    Mostly a factual prediction, hiding a definitions question: what counts as an "agency", and replacing which tasks? Pin down the definitions first, then ask what evidence would settle the prediction. Half of all business arguments are really definition fights.

    Day 2 · Psychology Psychology track · 1 of 12 about 20 min

    From skull bumps to science

    In the 1800s phrenologists read your personality off the bumps on your head, and people paid for it. Psychology became a science the moment it started measuring and testing claims instead of telling stories about them. That shift is still going on today.

    What makes psychology a science and not organised common sense?

    Guess firstIs Freud's psychoanalysis the scientific foundation of modern psychology?

    Show answer
    No. It shaped the vocabulary (the unconscious, defence mechanisms), but most of its specific claims are hard to test. The scientific core is experimental and statistical.

    Guess firstWhat year is usually given as psychology's birthday?

    Show answer
    1879, when Wilhelm Wundt opened his experimental lab in Leipzig.

    Behaviourismstudy only observable behaviour (Watson, Skinner)
    Cognitive revolution1950s-70s return to studying the mind's inner workings
    Levels of explanationthe same act explained by cells, a person or a culture

    Intro to Psychology

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The schools Hank runs through, and which ones survived
    • Where Freud sits, and how Hank handles him

    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • This series is from 2014, and that matters. In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration re-ran 100 published psychology studies: only 36% came out significant again (vs 97% originally), and effects were about half as big. Every psychology day in this guide carries a 2026 status check.
    • WEIRD samples. Most classic findings come from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic people, often US undergrads (Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan, 2010). For Indian family, workplace or caste contexts, the insider question is "does this transfer?"
    • Levels of explanation. A panic attack can be explained by amygdala circuits, by a person's learned fear, by a stressful job, or by a culture's norms. All can be true at once. "Neuro" isn't automatically deeper, just a different level.
    • Psychologist vs psychiatrist. Psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe. Clinical psychologists diagnose and run therapy. Research psychologists may never see a patient.
    Wilhelm WundtOpened the first psychology lab, Leipzig, 1879. Measured reaction times.
    William JamesPrinciples of Psychology (1890). Asked what the mind is for, not just what it's made of.

    "Is that from a preregistered replication, or one study from the 2000s?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: what makes psychology a science rather than common sense?

    Compare with a model answer
    It turns hunches into testable claims, measures behaviour carefully, compares conditions and checks whether results replicate. Common sense says both "opposites attract" and "birds of a feather flock together". Psychology asks which is true, for whom, and how big the effect really is.

    Why is 1879 psychology's birthday?

    Show answer
    Wilhelm Wundt opened the first experimental psychology lab in Leipzig.

    What did the 2015 replication project find?

    Show answer
    Of 100 studies, about 36% replicated with significant results (vs 97% originally), and effects were roughly half as large.

    What does WEIRD stand for, and why care?

    Show answer
    Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic. Most classic findings come from such samples, so they may not transfer to other cultures.

    A LinkedIn post says: "Studies show people decide in 7 seconds whether to trust a website." What three questions does an insider ask?

    Show a model answer
    Who were the participants, and how many? What exactly was measured (trust, or a quick rating of looks)? Has it replicated, and how big was the effect? Usually the answer is one small study, and the rating was of visual appeal.

    Day 3 · Philosophy Philosophy track · 2 of 16 about 20 min

    How to argue

    Most arguments you'll hear in a meeting are stories with a conclusion at the end. Philosophers take them apart like engineers: list the premises, check the shape, test each stone. Once you can do that out loud, you win more arguments by asking questions than by making claims.

    Review2 minPredict2 minWatch9:43Insider3 minRecall3 min
    1 · Warm-up review · 2 min

    Day 2 · 1 day agoWhat did the 2015 replication project find?

    Show answer
    Of 100 studies, about 36% replicated with significant results (vs 97% originally), and effects were roughly half as large.

    Day 1 · your last philosophy dayWhy do we only know Socrates second-hand?

    Show answer
    He wrote nothing. We know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, mostly Plato.
    2 · Predict first · 2 min

    What makes an argument good, and how do you take one apart politely?

    Guess firstTrue or false: a valid argument always has a true conclusion.

    Show answer
    False. Valid only means the shape works. "All fish fly; a salmon is a fish; so salmons fly" is perfectly valid and totally unsound.

    Guess firstDoes "begging the question" mean "raising the question"?

    Show answer
    Not in philosophy. It means circular reasoning: quietly assuming the very thing you're trying to prove.

    Five words to know before you press play:

    Premisea reason offered in support
    Conclusionwhat the reasons are meant to support
    Validif the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be
    Soundvalid AND every premise actually true
    Counterexampleone case that breaks a general claim

    How to Argue: Philosophical Reasoning

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • How Hank separates premises from the conclusion
    • The difference between valid and sound
    • How a single counterexample kills a general claim
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • The hidden premise is where arguments die. Real-world arguments leave a premise unstated (an enthymeme). Your job is to say it out loud: "So we're assuming the chatbot caused their growth?"
    • Charity first, then attack. Insiders steelman: restate the other side's strongest version before criticising it. It's more persuasive and it protects you from beating a straw man.
    • How philosophers actually talk: "I'm inclined to think...", "that doesn't entail...", "that objection undercuts premise two". Calm, specific, about the reasoning and never the person.
    • Don't throw fallacy names as insults. Shouting "ad hominem!" ends the conversation. Showing which premise fails moves it forward.
    Aristotle384-322 BCE. Invented formal logic (the syllogism). It ruled for 2,000 years.
    Gottlob FregeBegriffsschrift, 1879: modern logic is born the same year as Wundt's psychology lab.

    "Let's number the premises. Which one are we actually disagreeing about?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: the difference between valid and sound, with your own example.

    Compare with a model answer
    Valid means the conclusion follows if the premises are true; it's about shape. Sound means valid and the premises really are true. "Every Ahmedabad clinic needs a website; Riya's is an Ahmedabad clinic; so it needs one" is valid, but unsound if the first premise is false.

    Define a valid argument.

    Show answer
    One where, if the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false. It's about form, not truth.

    What's a hidden premise, and why hunt for it?

    Show answer
    An unstated assumption the argument needs. It's usually the weakest stone.

    What is steelmanning?

    Show answer
    Restating the opposing view in its strongest form before you criticise it.

    Client: "Our competitor added a chatbot and they're growing fast, so we need a chatbot." Number the premises and find the weak one.

    Show a model answer
    P1: the competitor added a chatbot. P2: the competitor is growing. Hidden P3: the chatbot caused the growth and would do the same for us. C: we need a chatbot. P3 is the weak stone, because it's correlation without evidence of cause. Ask what else changed for them.

    Day 4 · Psychology Psychology track · 2 of 12 about 20 min

    Real findings vs good stories

    In 1904 a horse called Clever Hans amazed Berlin by tapping out the answers to sums with his hoof. Experts were fooled. Then a young psychologist, Oskar Pfungst, noticed Hans only got it right when the questioner knew the answer. The horse was reading faces. That one story contains all of research methods.

    How do you tell a real finding from a convincing story?

    Guess firstCountries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel prizes (a real 2012 finding). Does chocolate make you smarter?

    Show answer
    No. Rich countries buy more chocolate and fund more research. Wealth is the confound.

    Guess firstWhat single feature lets an experiment show cause, not just correlation?

    Show answer
    Random assignment to conditions. It spreads every hidden factor evenly across the groups.

    Five words to know before you press play:

    Operational definitionexactly how a vague idea gets measured
    Correlationtwo things move together
    Random assignmenta coin flip decides who gets which condition
    Confounda hidden third factor that explains the link
    Double-blindneither participant nor experimenter knows who got what

    Psychological Research

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • His examples of correlation that isn't causation

    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Effect size beats "significant". Statistically significant only means unlikely to be pure chance. Insiders ask how big the effect is (Cohen's d, r) and how wide the uncertainty is.
    • p-hacking and HARKing. Trying analyses until something hits p < .05, then pretending you predicted it. This, plus small samples and publication bias, drove the replication crisis.
    • The fix: preregistration. Write down the hypothesis and the analysis before collecting data. Registered reports go further: the journal accepts the paper before the results exist.
    • The Clever Hans effect is now the name for experimenters leaking expectations. It's why double-blind trials exist, and it's exactly how cold-reading psychics work. Remember that for the cons course.
    Oskar PfungstDebunked Clever Hans in 1907 with controlled tests. A founding story of experimental control.
    Brian NosekCo-founded the Center for Open Science and led the 2015 replication project.

    "What's the effect size, and was it preregistered?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why correlation doesn't prove causation, using the chocolate and Nobel prizes example.

    Compare with a model answer
    Chocolate eating and Nobel prizes rise together across countries, but a third factor, national wealth, drives both. Rich countries buy more chocolate and fund more science. To show cause you need an experiment that randomly assigns the supposed cause, so hidden factors like wealth get spread evenly.

    What is a confound?

    Show answer
    A hidden third variable that causes both things you're comparing, making them look linked.

    Why did Clever Hans seem to do maths?

    Show answer
    He read tiny unconscious cues from questioners who knew the answer. Without a knowing questioner, he failed.

    What does preregistration prevent?

    Show answer
    Changing your hypothesis or analysis after seeing the data (p-hacking and HARKing).

    Callers using the new script booked more discovery calls last week. Before you switch the whole team, what do you check?

    Show a model answer
    Selection: did the better callers choose the new script? Randomly assign scripts across callers and leads for two weeks, decide in advance what counts as success, get enough calls per group, and watch for regression to the mean after one good week.

    Day 5 · Philosophy Philosophy track · 3 of 16 about 20 min

    Reasoning without certainty

    Deduction gives you certainty, and almost nothing in life comes with it. Detectives, doctors, debuggers and investors all reason from patterns and clues to the most likely story. Philosophers have names for these moves and a very old problem nobody has fully solved.

    Show answer

    2 · Predict first · 2 min

    How should you reason when certainty isn't on offer, which is almost always?

    Guess firstIs Sherlock Holmes's method mostly deduction?

    Show answer
    No, it's mostly abduction: inferring the best explanation of the clues. Conan Doyle used the wrong word.

    Guess firstThe sun has risen every day in recorded history. Does that prove it will rise tomorrow?

    Show answer
    Not logically. That's Hume's problem of induction. It's overwhelming inductive support, not proof.

    Five words to know before you press play:

    Deductionrule + case, so a certain result
    Inductionmany cases, so a probable rule
    Abductiona surprise, so the best available explanation
    Problem of inductionHume: past patterns can't logically guarantee future ones
    Defeasiblecould be overturned by new evidence

    How to Argue: Induction & Abduction

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • What makes an inductive argument strong or weak
    • How abduction differs from induction
    • Hank's criteria for picking the "best" explanation
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • What makes an explanation "best": it explains more of the evidence, assumes less (Occam's razor, with explanatory power held fixed), fits what we already know, and makes testable predictions.
    • Hume's problem (1739-48) still has no non-circular solution: any argument that induction works relies on induction. Insiders shrug and use it anyway, but stay humble about extrapolating.
    • Bayesian reasoning is abduction with numbers. Prior, likelihood, posterior: your MSc already speaks this language. Philosophers call it formal epistemology.
    • Indian parallel: Nyaya inference (anumana). The classic case: "there is fire on the hill, because there is smoke; wherever there's smoke there's fire, as in a kitchen." A five-step template for inference, about 2,000 years old.
    David Hume1711-1776. Showed induction can't justify itself, then got on with life.
    Charles Sanders Peirce1839-1914. Named abduction as its own kind of reasoning.

    "What's the best explanation here, and what would we expect to see if it's wrong?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: deduction vs induction vs abduction, with one example of each from your own work.

    Compare with a model answer
    Deduction: every client pays a 50% deposit, Riya's a client, so Riya paid a deposit. That's certain if true. Induction: the last nine Instagram leads replied within a day, so the next probably will. Abduction: bookings suddenly hit zero, and a broken form best explains it, so check the form first.

    Which kind of reasoning guarantees its conclusion if the premises are true?

    Show answer
    Deduction.

    State Hume's problem of induction in one line.

    Show answer
    Nothing logically guarantees the future will resemble the past, and any argument that it will uses induction itself.

    Nyaya's smoke-and-fire example: what kind of inference is it closest to?

    Show answer
    A careful induction or abduction backed by a general rule (wherever smoke, there's fire) and an example (the kitchen).

    Website conversions dropped 40% overnight. Give three explanations, ranked, and the cheapest first test.

    Show a model answer
    1. Tracking broke (sudden and total drops usually mean measurement). 2. The form or payment step is failing. 3. A traffic mix change (ad paused, algorithm update). The cheapest test: did visits change, and does the tracking tag still fire? Rule out measurement before you rethink the marketing.

    Day 6 · Psychology Psychology track · 3 of 12 about 20 min

    Fast and slow thinking

    Your fast mind handles most of life without you noticing: faces, language, danger, driving. It runs on shortcuts called heuristics. They're usually brilliant. Salespeople, ad designers and con artists earn their living in the moments they misfire. Today you learn to spot those moments.

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Replication status, 2026: anchoring is robust (the mechanism is debated). Framing is robust. Loss aversion is real but smaller and more conditional than the slogan says. Social priming (tiny cues causing big behaviour changes) largely failed to replicate.
    • Kahneman himself flagged it. In 2012 he warned priming researchers of a "train wreck looming", and in 2017 he wrote that he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies. Read that chapter of Thinking, Fast and Slow as history.
    • System 1 and 2 are a metaphor, not brain parts. No region is "System 2". Critics like Gerd Gigerenzer argue the biases-everywhere story underrates how good fast intuition is in the right environment.
    • Expertise retrains the hare. A chess master's fast intuition is reliable because they got years of rapid, clear feedback. A pundit's isn't, because they never did. Trust intuition only where feedback has been fast and honest.

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Popper isn't the last word. Kuhn (1962) showed real science works inside paradigms that resist refutation for a long time. Lakatos described research programmes with a protected core. The Duhem-Quine point: you never test a hypothesis alone, always with background assumptions.
    • Today's insider view: falsifiability is an excellent warning light, but not a complete definition of science. A claim that can't lose isn't science. A claim that can lose still needs good tests.
    • The replication crisis is Popper's revenge. Psychology spent decades publishing confirmations. Preregistration forces researchers to say in advance what result would prove them wrong. That's falsifiability in practice.
    • Week 1 tie-up: the scoreboard below sorts famous findings by how they survived serious testing.
    Karl Popper1902-1994. The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934). Science advances by bold guesses and attempted refutations.
    Thomas Kuhn1922-1996. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962). Coined "paradigm shift".

    "What result would change your mind? If nothing could, it isn't a hypothesis, it's a belief."

    A marketing guru says his funnel works for everyone, and when it fails it's because you didn't commit hard enough. What's wrong with that?

    Show a model answer
    It's unfalsifiable through an ad hoc rescue: every failure gets blamed on you, so the method can never lose. Ask him what result would show his funnel doesn't work, and for numbers from people who failed, not just testimonials from winners.
    Week 1 tie-up · the replication scoreboard

    Popper's test applied to the psychology you'll hear quoted most. Status as of October 2026, from multi-lab replications and meta-analyses.

    Held up
    • Classical and operant conditioning: robust, richer than the cartoons
    • Anchoring: robust; how it works is debated
    • Asch conformity: robust, varies by culture and stakes
    • CBT works for many anxiety and depressive disorders
    • Heritability: robust, and widely misread
    Mixed
    • Milgram: real, but read as engaged followership, not robots
    • Bystander effect: real; the Kitty Genovese story was wrong
    • Growth mindset: small effects, mainly for struggling students
    • Marshmallow test: shrinks a lot after family controls
    • Dunning-Kruger: partly a statistical artifact
    Failed or overstated
    • Stanford Prison Experiment as taught: guards were coached
    • Power posing hormone claims
    • Social priming (slow walking after 'elderly' words)
    • Ego depletion as a fuel tank: near-zero in big trials
    • Learning styles, 10% of the brain, left vs right-brained people

    Week 1 boss fight (optional, 10 min). Take the claim "Two minutes of power posing raises testosterone and makes you take bolder risks" and run the whole week's toolkit on it.

    Show a model answer
    Kind of claim: empirical and causal. Premises: posture changes hormones, hormones change risk-taking, so posture changes risk-taking. Evidence ladder: one small 2010 study (rung 4, no preregistration). Confounds: demand characteristics (participants guess the point), tiny samples. Falsification test: a larger replication (Ranehill et al., 2015) found no hormone or risk effect. Verdict: the headline claim failed. A small effect on how confident people say they feel may survive. Say it in the room: "Nice story, but the hormone effect didn't replicate."

    CalibrationRate yourself 1 to 5 again: could you explain to a CEO what psychology and philosophy study, and how they differ? Compare it with your Day 1 number.

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Predictive processing is the 2026 frame. Many researchers now describe the brain as a prediction machine: it guesses what's out there and uses the senses mainly to correct the guess (prediction error). Helmholtz called it "unconscious inference" in the 1860s. Insider caution: it's a family of models, not one confirmed mechanism.
    • The Dress (2015) split the internet into blue-black vs white-gold. Same photo, different brains making different assumptions about the lighting. One study linked white-gold viewers to assuming daylight, and even to being early risers (Wallisch, 2017).
    • Attention is a spotlight. In the invisible gorilla study (Simons and Chabris, 1999), about half of the people counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. It has been replicated many times. Outside the spotlight, your brain is filling in.
    • Culture tunes perception. In the 1960s, Segall, Campbell and Herskovits reported that people raised among right-angled buildings fall for the Muller-Lyer illusion more than people from some rural communities. How big the cultural gap really is is still debated, but it's a classic WEIRD warning.
    Hermann von Helmholtz1821-1894. Physicist and physiologist who called perception "unconscious inference", long before computers.
    Max WertheimerCo-founded Gestalt psychology in 1912 with the phi phenomenon: still images that look like motion, the basis of every film.

    "Are we looking at the data, or at what we expected the data to say?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why is perception better described as a guess than a recording?

    Compare with a model answer
    Your senses deliver patchy, noisy signals, so the brain combines them with expectations from memory and context to build its best guess of what's out there. Usually the guess is fast and excellent. Illusions, the Dress and the missed gorilla show the machinery at work: what you see depends on what you expect and where your attention points.

    What's the difference between bottom-up and top-down processing?

    Show answer
    Bottom-up builds perception from raw sensory signals. Top-down uses expectations, knowledge and context to interpret them.

    What did the invisible gorilla study show?

    Show answer
    About half of people busy counting passes didn't notice a person in a gorilla suit. Attention limits what reaches awareness: inattentional blindness.

    What did Helmholtz call perception?

    Show answer
    Unconscious inference: the brain infers the most likely cause of its sensory signals.

    You show a dental clinic owner two homepage mockups. He says the second one "looks cheaper", but it's the same layout with a different hero photo. What's going on, and how do you use it?

    Show a model answer
    Top-down processing. The photo set his expectations (a perceptual set), and he read the rest of the page through that lens. Use it on purpose: the hero image and first headline prime how everything below gets judged, so test those first, not the footer.

    Cartesian Skepticism: Neo, Meet Rene

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Almost nobody accepts Descartes' way back. He rebuilt the world by proving a good God who wouldn't deceive us. Antoine Arnauld spotted the problem in 1641, now called the Cartesian circle: Descartes needs clear ideas to prove God, and God to trust clear ideas.
    • Insiders separate certainty from knowledge. Most epistemologists today are fallibilists: you can know things without being infallible. G.E. Moore's 1939 reply holds up his hands: I'm more sure that here is one hand than I am of any premise in the sceptic's argument.
    • Older than Descartes, and not only European. Greek Pyrrhonists like Sextus Empiricus suspended judgement for peace of mind. The Chinese Daoist Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and woke unsure which one he was. Indian traditions ask the dream question too, through ideas like maya.
    • Simulation theory is the 2026 version. Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument says one of three things is true, one being that we're probably in a simulation. It's a probability argument about future civilisations, not a proof. David Chalmers (Reality+, 2022) argues that even a simulated world is still real enough to know things in.
    Rene Descartes1596-1650. Meditations on First Philosophy (1641). Father of modern philosophy, and of the x-y graph you used in maths.
    Zhuangzi4th century BCE Daoist. The butterfly dream: am I a man who dreamt of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming I'm a man?

    Compare with a model answer
    He doubted everything that could possibly be false: the senses (illusions), being awake (dreams), even maths (an evil deceiving demon). One thing survived: while doubting, he must be thinking, so he must exist. From that foundation he tried to rebuild knowledge, but his route back, through a God who doesn't deceive, convinces few philosophers today.

    Show answer

    Show answer
    Descartes uses clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, then uses God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. The argument goes in a circle.

    What is fallibilism?

    Show answer
    The view that you can know things without being absolutely certain of them. It's the mainstream position in epistemology today.

    Show a model answer
    Possibility isn't probability, the same move as answering the sceptic. Ask what the realistic threat is, how likely it is and what it would cost. Then match the defence to the risk. Descartes' method makes great threat modelling (imagine the worst deceiver) and a terrible buying rule.

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Networks, not boxes. "The amygdala is the fear centre" and "the frontal lobe is the CEO" are useful cartoons. Modern neuroscience talks about distributed networks: the default mode network, the salience network, the control network. Insiders say "involved in", never "the centre of".
    • fMRI is powerful and easy to oversell. It measures blood oxygen, a slow and indirect signal, and needs heavy statistics. In 2009 researchers "found" activity in a dead salmon to show what happens without proper correction (Bennett et al.). Linking scans to traits like IQ needs thousands of people, not dozens (Marek et al., Nature, 2022).
    • Phineas Gage is real but over-told. In 1848 an iron rod went through the railway foreman's frontal lobe and he survived. The "his personality changed forever" version got embellished over time. Later evidence suggests he partly recovered and drove stagecoaches in Chile.
    • Neurobabble persuades. People rate bad explanations as better when irrelevant neuroscience is added (Weisberg et al., 2008, "the seductive allure"). When a pitch deck says "neuro", ask what the brain data adds that behaviour data doesn't.
    Santiago Ramon y Cajal1852-1934. Proved the brain is made of separate cells (the neuron doctrine). Nobel Prize 1906. His drawings are still used in textbooks.
    Paul BrocaLinked a left frontal region to speech production in 1861, from a patient who could only say one syllable, "tan".

Brains work as distributed networks, and an fMRI "light-up" is a slow, indirect, averaged signal. "Involved in" is accurate. "Centre of" is a headline.

    Show answer
    People find weak explanations more convincing when irrelevant neuroscience is added.

    An agency pitches your client "neuromarketing websites proven to trigger the brain's buying centre". What do you ask?

    Show a model answer
    Which study, how many people, and what was measured? There's no single buying centre. If the evidence is a lab scan of 20 people, an ordinary A/B test on real visitors tells you more. The neuro language is the seductive allure effect, used as a sales tool.

    When is a lucky guess not knowledge?

    For about 2,000 years the standard answer was: knowledge is a belief that is true and justified. Then in 1963 Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper with two counterexamples, and philosophers have been trying to patch the definition ever since.

    Day 4 · 7 days agoWhat is a confound?

    Show answer
    A hidden third variable that causes both things you're comparing, making them look linked.

    Day 9 · your last philosophy dayWhat are Descartes' three doubts, in order?

    Show answer

    Show answer
    You never test a hypothesis alone: a failed test might be blaming a background assumption instead.

    Day 3 · four philosophy days backDefine a valid argument.

    Show answer
    One where, if the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false. It's about form, not truth.

    What has to be added to a true belief to turn it into knowledge?

    Guess firstTrue or false: if you believe something true and have a good reason for it, you know it.

    Show answer
    That was the textbook view until 1963. Gettier showed cases where all three hold and it still isn't knowledge, because luck disconnects your reason from the truth.

    Guess firstHow long was Gettier's famous paper?

    Show answer
    About three pages. It's one of the most cited short papers in philosophy, and he barely published anything else.

    Gettier casea justified true belief that is true only by luck

    The Meaning of Knowledge

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • The three conditions of the classic definition

    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Gettier wasn't first. Around the 8th century CE the Indian Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara described a traveller who sees a mirage of water, and when he reaches the spot there happens to be real water under a rock. Insiders now credit Indian epistemology with spotting the problem more than a thousand years earlier.
    • Nobody has a patch everyone accepts. Candidates include no false lemmas, reliabilism (Alvin Goldman), safety (your belief couldn't easily have been wrong) and virtue epistemology (Ernest Sosa, Linda Zagzebski). Timothy Williamson flipped the project: maybe knowledge is basic and can't be split into parts ("knowledge first").
    • Experimental philosophers tested the intuition. A 2001 study suggested Gettier intuitions vary by culture. A bigger 2017 study (Machery et al.) found people in Brazil, India, Japan and the US share the intuition that a Gettier case isn't knowledge.
    • Founders meet Gettier every week. Sign-ups jumped the week you changed the headline, so you "know" the headline worked. Maybe a rival's site was down that week. True belief, decent justification, connected by luck.
    Edmund Gettier1927-2021. Wrote "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" (1963), reportedly to secure tenure, and became famous for three pages.
    Dharmottara8th-century Buddhist philosopher in the tradition of Dharmakirti. His mirage case anticipates Gettier.

    "Were we right because of the evidence, or did we just get lucky?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: what is a Gettier case, and why did it matter?

    Compare with a model answer
    A Gettier case is a belief that is true and justified, yet true only by luck, so it doesn't count as knowledge. A stopped clock that happens to show the right time is the classic example. Gettier's 1963 paper broke the 2,000-year-old definition of knowledge as justified true belief, and no proposed fix is universally accepted.

    What are the three conditions in the classic definition of knowledge?

    Show answer
    Belief, truth and justification: justified true belief.

    Give the stopped clock case in one sentence.

    Show answer
    You read a stopped clock that happens to show the right time: your belief is true and justified, but only by luck.

    What does reliabilism say?

    Show answer
    A belief counts as knowledge if a reliable process produced it (like good eyesight in good light), even if you can't spell out your reasons.

    Your callers booked 9 discovery calls on the day you changed their opening line. Do you know the new line works?

    Show a model answer
    Not yet. That's Gettier-shaped: you might be right, but the evidence doesn't connect to the truth. A post-holiday Monday, one caller's warm list or plain chance could explain it. Run the new line for two weeks against the old one on the same lead segments. Then you'll know, not guess.

    Why can a vivid, confident memory still be wrong?

    Guess firstTrue or false: a very confident eyewitness is probably accurate.

    Show answer
    Partly false. Confidence at a first, fair identification carries real information (Wixted and Wells, 2017), but confidence grows with time, feedback and retelling. Mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in about 69% of US wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA.

    Guess firstCan you plant a memory of something that never happened?

    Show answer
    In some people, yes. In Loftus's "lost in the mall" study (1995), about a quarter of participants came to remember, at least partly, a childhood event that never happened.

    Interferenceold learning blocks new (proactive), or new blocks old (retroactive)
    Misinformation effectdetails suggested after an event get blended into the memory
    Reconsolidationa recalled memory becomes editable before it's stored again

    Remembering and Forgetting

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • Recall vs recognition, and why multiple choice feels easier
    • How context, mood and priming bring memories back
    • The car-crash experiment and what one verb did to people's memories
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Loftus and Palmer (1974). People who watched a car crash film gave higher speed estimates when asked how fast the cars "smashed" rather than "hit" each other. A week later more of them falsely remembered broken glass. One verb rewrote the memory, and courts now treat leading questions seriously because of this line of work.
    • The memory wars. In the 1990s, therapy using hypnosis and suggestion "recovered" memories of abuse, some of them demonstrably false, which led to lawsuits. Most memory researchers are sceptical of repressed-and-recovered memories, while some clinicians defend dissociative amnesia. Insiders separate "trauma is real" from "this retrieval method is reliable".
    • This guide runs on memory science. Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve on himself in 1885, and retrieval practice (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006) is one of the strongest findings in psychology. That's why you test yourself before you look at the answer.
    • Patient HM. Henry Molaison lost both hippocampi to surgery in 1953 and couldn't form new long-term memories. Yet he got better at a mirror-drawing task without remembering any practice. That's how we know memory is several systems: explicit (facts and events) and implicit (skills and habits).
    Elizabeth LoftusShowed how memories are edited by suggestion. Hugely influential, and controversial for testifying as an expert witness in high-profile trials.
    Hermann Ebbinghaus1850-1909. Memorised thousands of nonsense syllables to map the forgetting curve on himself.

    "Let's check the call notes, not what we remember from the call."

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: why can a confident memory be wrong?

    Compare with a model answer
    Remembering isn't playback. You rebuild the event from fragments each time, and the rebuild can absorb later information, leading questions and retellings: the misinformation effect. Confidence grows with repetition, not accuracy. Loftus showed one word, "smashed" instead of "hit", raised speed estimates and planted broken glass. Treat vivid memories as reconstructions, especially old or often-told ones.

    What did Loftus and Palmer change in 1974, and what happened?

    Show answer
    The verb in the question, "smashed" vs "hit". "Smashed" raised speed estimates and produced more false memories of broken glass.

    What does the forgetting curve show?

    Show answer
    Memory drops steeply soon after learning, then levels off. Spaced reviews flatten it.

    What did patient HM teach us?

    Show answer
    Memory has separate systems: he couldn't form new explicit memories but could still learn motor skills implicitly.

    A caller says a dentist "definitely said call back Thursday at 4". The dentist says he never agreed. How do you stop this happening again?

    Show a model answer
    Both memories are reconstructions, so don't play judge. Fix the record instead. Callers log the exact time and words in the sheet during the call, then send a WhatsApp confirmation straight after: "Confirming a 10-minute call with Kevin, Thursday 4 pm." A same-day written confirmation beats anyone's memory.

    Where Does Your Mind Reside?

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • Descartes' argument that mind and body are different things
    • What reductive physicalism claims, and what it struggles with
    • "Mysterianism": the view that we may never solve this
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia landed the knockout question in letters to Descartes in 1643: how can an immaterial soul move a material body? His replies never satisfied her. It's still called the interaction problem, and it's why few philosophers are substance dualists today.
    • The hard problem. David Chalmers (1995) split the "easy" problems (explaining attention, memory and report, which are hard but doable) from the hard problem: why any of it feels like something. Plenty of physicalists accept that the mind is the brain and still argue about whether that explains experience.
    • Functionalism is the AI connection. If mental states are defined by their roles, a mind could in principle run on silicon. John Searle's Chinese Room (1980) argues that running the right program isn't enough for understanding. In 2026 some philosophers and AI labs treat AI consciousness as a serious research question, while most scientists think today's chatbots aren't conscious.
    • India's map has extra options. Samkhya is dualist but puts the thinking mind (manas, buddhi) on the matter side: only pure consciousness (purusha) is separate. Advaita Vedanta makes consciousness fundamental, a distant cousin of panpsychism, which about 8% of philosophers now accept or lean towards.
    Elisabeth of Bohemia1618-1680. Her letters exposed the interaction problem in Descartes' view, and his answers never satisfied her.
    David ChalmersAustralian philosopher at NYU. Named "the hard problem of consciousness" in 1995.

    "Are we saying the AI understands, or that it behaves as if it understands? Those are different claims."

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: what's the mind-body problem, and what are the two main answers?

    Compare with a model answer
    It asks how thoughts and feelings relate to the physical brain. Dualists like Descartes say the mind is a separate, non-physical thing, but then struggle to explain how it moves the body. Physicalists, the majority today, say the mind is what the brain does, but struggle to explain why brain activity feels like anything: Chalmers' hard problem.

    What is the interaction problem?

    Show answer
    If the mind is non-physical, how can it cause physical changes in the body? Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed it against Descartes.

    What does functionalism say, and why does it matter for AI?

    Show answer
    A mental state is defined by its causal role, not its material, so in principle a mind could run on silicon.

    What's the hard problem of consciousness?

    Show answer
    Explaining why physical processing comes with subjective experience at all, not just how the brain processes information.

    A dentist asks: "Does your AI receptionist actually understand my patients?" What's the honest insider answer?

    Show a model answer
    Separate behaviour from understanding. "In the practical sense, yes: it books, answers FAQs and hands off in Gujarati and Hindi. Whether it understands like a person is an open question, so we built it to pass anything unusual to your staff." It's honest, and it sells better than overclaiming.

    Consciousness

    Opens on YouTube. Watch it straight through, then come back for the insider layer.

    Watch for:

    • How Hank defines consciousness, and the two tracks of dual processing
    • Selective attention and the cocktail party effect
    • Inattentional and change blindness (you met the gorilla on Day 8)
    4 · The insider layer · 3 min

    What Crash Course doesn't tell you

    • An adversarial collaboration. Supporters of two rival theories, global workspace and integrated information, agreed predictions in advance and ran a joint experiment (the Cogitate consortium). Results reported in 2023 and published in Nature in 2025 challenged key predictions of both. In 2023 over 100 researchers also signed a letter calling integrated information theory pseudoscience, which set off a major row.
    • Nagel's phrase is the insider definition. In "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (1974), an organism is conscious if there is something it is like to be it. Use that phrase and people know you've read the literature.
    • Processing without awareness is real. Blindsight patients, with damage to the visual cortex, say they see nothing in part of their visual field, yet can point to objects there far better than chance (Lawrence Weiskrantz). Seeing and being aware of seeing can come apart.
    • It matters in hospitals. Researchers measure how complex the brain's "echo" is after a magnetic pulse (the perturbational complexity index) to detect hidden awareness in unresponsive patients. Consciousness science isn't only seminar talk.
    Thomas NagelAmerican philosopher. "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" (1974) defined consciousness as there being something it is like to be you.
    Anil SethSussex neuroscientist. Being You (2021): perception and the self as a "controlled hallucination".

    "Are we talking about experience itself, or just what people can report?"

    5 · Recall and use it · 3 min

    Explain it, video closedIn 60 words: what is consciousness, and why is it so hard to study?

    Compare with a model answer
    Consciousness is there being something it is like to be you: awareness of yourself and the world. Science can study its measurable side, such as attention, reports, sleep and brain correlates, but experience itself is only visible from the inside. Rival theories make different predictions, and a careful head-to-head test hasn't crowned a winner yet. Nagel's bat captures the gap.

    What is Nagel's test for whether a creature is conscious?

    Show answer
    There is something it is like to be that creature.

    What is blindsight?

    Show answer
    Patients with visual cortex damage report seeing nothing, yet can locate objects far better than chance: processing without awareness.

    What was unusual about the Cogitate study?

    Show answer
    It was an adversarial collaboration: rival theorists agreed predictions in advance. Neither theory came out cleanly confirmed.

    You're writing the AI receptionist's opening line. What does attention research say about the first five seconds of a call?

    Show a model answer
    People filter hard, and only things they care about cut through, like their name or their problem (the cocktail party effect). Lead with that: "Hi, this is Smile Dental. I can book or move your appointment right now." Skip the long welcome. Attention is a narrow spotlight and you get one shot at it.
    Week 2 tie-up · seven ways knowing goes wrong

    One line per day. Together they are your toolkit for any claim about what's real.

    DayThe lessonSay it in the room
    Perceptionguesses"Is that the signal, or what we expected?"
    Scepticismpossibility is not probability"What would make that likely?"
    The brainpick the right level"Circuit, person or situation?"
    Knowledgebeware lucky truths"Right because of the evidence, or luck?"
    Memoryrebuilds"Check the notes, not the memory."
    Mindbehaviour is not understanding"Understands, or acts as if?"
    Consciousnessreport is not experience"Experience, or what people can report?"

    Week 2 boss fight (optional, 10 min). A rival agency's pitch to your dental clients says: "Our AI receptionist truly understands your patients, remembers every caller, and never mishears." Run the whole week on it.

    Show a model answer
    Perception (Day 8): speech recognition is a best guess too, so "never mishears" is false; Gujarati-English code-switching on a bad line will trip it. Scepticism (Day 9): ask for the error rate on real calls, not a demo. Brain (Day 10): "understands" at which level, word matching or the patient's actual need? Knowledge (Day 11): a correct booking from a lucky guess isn't reliability; ask how it handles ambiguity. Memory (Day 12): "remembers" means stored logs, which raises consent and data questions. Mind and consciousness (Days 13-14): it behaves as if it understands; nothing is experienced. Your counter-pitch: "Ours is honest about its limits: it handles 80% of routine calls and hands the rest to your front desk." Measure that 80% on your own pilot before you say it.

    CalibrationRate yourself 1 to 5: could you explain to a client the difference between seeing, knowing and remembering, and why each can fail? Compare it with your Week 1 number.

    Glossary · Weeks 1-2 + map

    Field glossary

    AbductionPhilosophy

    Inference to the best explanation.

    Ad hoc rescuePhilosophy

    An excuse invented to save a claim from contrary evidence.

    Analytic philosophyPhilosophy

    Style prizing explicit argument, distinctions and formal tools.

    AnchoringPsychology

    The first number biases later estimates.

    Availability heuristicPsychology

    Judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind.

    Base ratePsychology

    How common something is in the population overall.

    Begging the questionPhilosophy

    Circular reasoning: assuming what you set out to prove.

    BehaviourismPsychology

    Watson and Skinner: study observable behaviour and conditioning.

    BlindsightPsychology

    Responding to visual stimuli without reported awareness of seeing them.

    Bottom-up processingPsychology

    Building perception from raw sensory data.

    Brain in a vatPhilosophy

    Thought experiment: all experience fed in by a computer.

    Cartesian circlePhilosophy

    Using clear ideas to prove God, and God to trust clear ideas.

    Change blindnessPsychology

    Failing to notice large changes in a scene.

    Chinese RoomPhilosophy

    Searle: running the right program is not understanding.

    Clever Hans effectPsychology

    Subjects picking up unintended cues from the experimenter.

    Cocktail party effectPsychology

    Your name cutting through a noisy room.

    CogitoPhilosophy

    "I think, therefore I am": the belief doubt cannot touch.

    Cognitive revolutionPsychology

    1950s-70s return to studying memory, language and thought.

    ConfoundPsychology

    A hidden third variable that explains an apparent link.

    Continental philosophyPhilosophy

    Phenomenology, existentialism, critical theory: experience, history, power.

    CounterexamplePhilosophy

    A single case that breaks a general claim.

    DeductionPhilosophy

    Certain conclusions from premises, if they are true.

    Default mode networkPsychology

    Brain network active during mind-wandering and self-reflection.

    Demarcation problemPhilosophy

    Where to draw the line between science and non-science.

    Double-blindPsychology

    Neither participants nor experimenters know who got what.

    Duhem-Quine thesisPhilosophy

    Hypotheses are always tested together with background assumptions.

    Ecological rationalityPsychology

    Gigerenzer: a heuristic's quality depends on its environment.

    Effect sizePsychology

    How big an effect is, not just whether it exists.

    EnthymemePhilosophy

    An argument with an unstated, hidden premise.

    Epistemic luckPhilosophy

    Being right for the wrong reasons.

    EpistemologyPhilosophy

    The theory of knowledge and justified belief.

    Explicit vs implicit memoryPsychology

    Facts and events you can state vs skills and habits you show.

    FallibilismPhilosophy

    Knowledge without absolute certainty.

    FalsifiabilityPhilosophy

    A claim is scientific if some observation could show it false.

    fMRIPsychology

    Imaging blood oxygen changes as a slow proxy for brain activity.

    Forgetting curvePsychology

    Ebbinghaus: rapid early forgetting that then levels off.

    FoundationalismPhilosophy

    Knowledge rests on certain, basic foundations.

    Framing effectPsychology

    Equivalent options chosen differently depending on wording.

    FunctionalismPsychology

    William James: what the mind is for.

    GestaltPsychology

    Organising perception into wholes: figure-ground, proximity, closure.

    Gettier casePhilosophy

    A justified true belief that is true only by luck.

    Global workspace theoryPsychology

    Consciousness as information broadcast across the brain.

    Hard problemPhilosophy

    Why physical processing comes with experience at all.

    HARKingPsychology

    Hypothesising after the results are known.

    HeuristicPsychology

    A fast mental shortcut that is usually good enough.

    Inattentional blindnessPsychology

    Missing an obvious object when attention is elsewhere.

    InductionPhilosophy

    Probable generalisations from observed cases.

    Interaction problemPhilosophy

    How a non-physical mind could move a physical body.

    Justified true beliefPhilosophy

    The classic three-part definition of knowledge.

    Levels of explanationPsychology

    Cell, circuit, person, group and culture accounts of one behaviour.

    Limbic systemPsychology

    Amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus: emotion and memory.

    LogicPhilosophy

    The study of which inferences preserve truth or support.

    MetaphysicsPhilosophy

    What is real: mind, self, time, causation, God.

    Method of doubtPhilosophy

    Descartes: reject any belief that could possibly be false.

    Misinformation effectPsychology

    Post-event suggestions blending into a memory.

    MysterianismPhilosophy

    The view that humans may never solve the mind-body problem.

    NeuroplasticityPsychology

    The brain's lifelong capacity to rewire with experience.

    Occam's razorPhilosophy

    Prefer fewer assumptions, explanatory power held fixed.

    Operational definitionPsychology

    The exact procedure used to measure a concept.

    p-hackingPsychology

    Trying analyses until a result crosses p < .05.

    ParadigmPhilosophy

    Kuhn: the shared framework a scientific field works within.

    Perceptual setPsychology

    A mental readiness to perceive one thing over another.

    PhilPapers SurveyPhilosophy

    2009 and 2020 surveys of what professional philosophers believe.

    PhysicalismPhilosophy

    Everything, minds included, is physical or depends on the physical.

    PramanaPhilosophy

    Indian philosophy: a reliable source of knowledge (perception, inference, testimony...).

    Predictive processingPsychology

    The brain as a prediction machine corrected by sensory error signals.

    PremisePhilosophy

    A reason offered in support of a conclusion.

    PreregistrationPsychology

    Recording hypotheses and analyses before seeing data.

    Problem of inductionPhilosophy

    Hume: no non-circular justification for expecting the future to resemble the past.

    QualiaPhilosophy

    What an experience feels like from the inside.

    Random assignmentPsychology

    Assigning conditions by chance so groups are comparable.

    ReconsolidationPsychology

    A retrieved memory becoming editable before re-storage.

    Regression to the meanPsychology

    Extreme results tend to be followed by more average ones.

    ReliabilismPhilosophy

    Knowledge as belief produced by a reliable process.

    Replication crisisPsychology

    2011-15 discovery that many famous findings did not reproduce.

    RepresentativenessPsychology

    Judging by resemblance to a type, neglecting base rates.

    ScepticismPhilosophy

    Doubt about whether we can know some or all things.

    Seductive allurePsychology

    Bad explanations seem better with irrelevant neuroscience added.

    Selective attentionPsychology

    Focusing on one input and filtering the rest.

    Socratic methodPhilosophy

    Cross-examining someone to expose hidden assumptions.

    SoundPhilosophy

    Valid with all premises actually true.

    SteelmanPhilosophy

    The strongest version of the opposing view.

    StructuralismPsychology

    Wundt and Titchener: breaking experience into elements.

    Substance dualismPhilosophy

    Mind and body as two different kinds of thing.

    System 1 / System 2Psychology

    Kahneman's metaphor for fast intuition and slow deliberation.

    Top-down processingPsychology

    Expectations and knowledge shaping perception.

    ValidPhilosophy

    If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be.

    Value theoryPhilosophy

    Ethics, political philosophy and aesthetics.

    WEIRDPsychology

    Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic samples.

    Colophon

    Notice it. Question it. Use it.

Built on Crash Course Psychology (Hank Green, 2014) and Crash Course Philosophy (Hank Green, 2016-17), with an insider layer from replication studies, the PhilPapers Surveys, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and learning science (retrieval, spacing, pretesting, interleaving). Status labels reflect the evidence as of 4 October 2026.
